chapter: Last years of the band and reflections
title: Apollo Theater: lost music in 1946 and the nursery-rhyme closer of 1945
summary: In 1946 the band's music is lost in transit and the Apollo date goes poorly, while in 1945 a corny nursery-rhyme finale won the audience, including Sugar Ray Robinson.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Yes, with the extra it changed, huh? (unintelligible). And we played the date. That was in 1946. Apollo We booked ourselves back in the Apollo Theater. And this was a time when they lost our music. We sent our music out by Bail-

way Express. We got to New York, they didn't know where the music was. In other words, we couldn't rehearse, we couldn't get our thing -- we were lost. Didn't have our music. So finally we found the music the day we were supposed to open, that Friday. They found that the music was way up at Harlem, in some railway express company up there. So we rushed up there and we got our music and we get down, and we just got our music open -- I hadn't had a chance to pick out the tunes we were going to use in the show or nothing.
And we had to hit by 15 minutes. So the result of that trip, the band didn't do so hot, at the Apollo. The year we played the Apollo Theater, with Louis Jordan in 1945, the band was a riot.
But your lifesaver on that trip was Lucille Agers.
You mean this last trip. The '46 trip?
Yeah, when she whistled.
That's right.
That kind of saved you there.

She sure did. She broke it up. She broke it up. She did. But the trip before, in 1945, I had to beg the guys to use the songs we used overseas. I'll explain it to you. It was a nursery rhyme song. 'Go in and out the window, go in and out the window, go in and out the window, la la la la la. Then we had another tune, 'Last night, the
night before, 24 hours at the door. Open the door, let him in, hit him in the head with a rolling pin." That was our punch one we'd use on the end, see.

And the guys didn't want to use it, it was too corny. I begged them, I said, "Fellows, just do me this one favor. Just one favor. Do what I say to do. And if it's a failure, I'll give in. But just give it all you got." I said, "Let's do this number. Let's stand up and put our hearts in it."

We closed with that tune, and the other acts couldn't come on, could they, Charles? That was all she wrote. We finished that tune, and they stood up in the seats. Because we had all the nursery rhymes, but we played them all in rhythm, see. But, see, we built it up as we went along. We built it up. Kept building it, see, and then we got on the last one, was "Last night, the night before," see. And then we said, "24 hours at my door," everybody was hitting everybody over the head with a piece of paper or something, you know what I mean.
And, boy, the people were -- what's the boxer's name? The boxer that was so popular? Had a place on Seventh Avenue.
Sugar Ray.
Sugar Ray Robinson was just dying.
He was sitting on the ringside. Sugar Ray Robinson was sitting there, he was -- he was --
I'm trying to think, did we use that "Mushi mushi (unintelligible)." We didn't use that. We didn't use that.
We used that over in Japan.
We used that in Japan.
"London bridge" Mush, mush, ... Ah-no-way
MR. C. PILLARS: (Unintelligible.)

Mushy, mushy, yeah. We used that over there. See, we used that to add a little Japanese to it. Because quite a few Japanese would come to all those shows we played in Japan, see. And we sang that, boy, the Japanese, they fell in love with it. They just clapped.
